body:
Why was GSLV developed?

GSLV stands for Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. The operational vehicle generally referred to as GSLV in current mission descriptions is GSLV Mark II (GSLV Mk II). It was developed to provide India with a launch capability suited to heavier communication and other satellites requiring high-energy transfer orbits.

Many communication and navigation satellites need geosynchronous or geostationary operating orbits. Reaching these orbits generally requires a more demanding launch and spacecraft-propulsion sequence than placing a similar payload into low Earth orbit. GSLV addresses this requirement through a three-stage configuration that includes an indigenous cryogenic upper stage.

The 3 stages of GSLV Mk II

  1. First stage, GS1: A large solid-propellant core motor is assisted by 4 liquid-propellant L40 strap-on boosters. The strap-ons are part of the first-stage propulsion arrangement, not 4 additional sequential stages.
  2. Second stage, GS2: A liquid-propellant stage powered by a Vikas engine continues the ascent.
  3. Third stage, CUS: An indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage powered by the CE-7.5 engine provides the high-energy final acceleration needed for missions such as GTO insertion.

GSLV Mk II's use of liquid strap-on boosters is an important difference from PSLV, whose strap-on boosters are solid-propellant motors.

What makes the upper stage cryogenic?

A cryogenic propulsion system uses propellants stored at very low temperatures. The GSLV Mk II upper stage uses liquid hydrogen as fuel and liquid oxygen as oxidiser. An oxidiser supplies the oxygen needed for combustion, allowing the engine to operate without atmospheric oxygen.

The combination is efficient for producing the high velocity needed in the upper part of a launch. For prelims, the essential association is GSLV Mk II: indigenous cryogenic upper stage, CE-7.5 engine, liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.

Early GSLV flights used Russian-supplied cryogenic stages. A major technological milestone was the successful GSLV-D5/GSAT-14 mission on 5 January 2014, which used India's indigenous cryogenic upper stage.

Payload capability and usual orbit

ISRO specifies a capacity of about 2,250 kg to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit for GSLV Mk II. Its published low Earth orbit capability is much higher, about 6,000 kg, illustrating why two capacity figures must always be compared for the same destination orbit.

During a typical geosynchronous transfer mission, the rocket releases the satellite into an elliptical GTO. The satellite subsequently performs its own orbit-raising manoeuvres to reach its intended operating orbit.

GSLV does not necessarily mean GEO. The rocket usually places a suitable payload into GTO, not directly into a circular geostationary orbit. It can also serve missions to other orbits when configured for them.

Important GSLV missions

DateFlightSignificance
18 April 2001GSLV-D1First flight of the GSLV programme.
5 January 2014GSLV-D5Successfully launched GSAT-14 using an indigenous cryogenic upper stage.
17 February 2024GSLV-F14Launched the INSAT-3DS meteorological satellite towards GTO.
29 January 2025GSLV-F15Placed the navigation satellite NVS-02 into GTO; marked the 100th launch from Sriharikota.
30 July 2025GSLV-F16Launched the joint NASA–ISRO NISAR Earth-observation satellite into a Sun-synchronous polar orbit.
30 October 2026GSLV-F18Successfully placed the navigation satellite NVS-03 into GTO.

NISAR: an important exception to remember

NISAR stands for NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. It is an Earth-observation mission designed to measure changes on Earth's surface. GSLV-F16 launched it into a Sun-synchronous polar orbit at approximately 740 km altitude.

This example shows why an examiner cannot infer a satellite's actual orbit solely from the launch vehicle's name. Although GSLV was developed primarily for geosynchronous transfer missions, it can launch an Earth-observation satellite into a suitable polar orbit.

Successful launch versus successful spacecraft operation

GSLV-F15 successfully injected NVS-02 into its intended transfer orbit in January 2025. However, the spacecraft could not complete the required subsequent orbit raising. ISRO's 2026 investigation identified a problem involving the electrical drive signal to a valve in the spacecraft's orbit-raising propulsion system.

The distinction is crucial: the launch vehicle completed its assigned insertion, while the spacecraft encountered a later problem. A problem after separation should not automatically be described as a rocket-launch failure.

Latest verified example: GSLV-F18/NVS-03

On 30 October 2026, GSLV-F18, the 20th GSLV flight, successfully inserted NVS-03 into an elliptical geosynchronous transfer orbit. ISRO reported an initial orbit of approximately 170.3 km by 38,080 km, demonstrating the large difference between a transfer orbit's perigee and apogee.

An ISRO update dated 31 October 2026 confirmed successful completion of the spacecraft's first planned orbit-raising manoeuvre and stated that further manoeuvres were planned. The verified result at the 4 November 2026 content cutoff is the successful launch and transfer-orbit insertion; this should not be confused with a claim that final geosynchronous positioning or full navigation service had already been completed.

Prelims focus

  • GSLV Mk II has 3 sequential stages and 4 liquid strap-on boosters.
  • Its first-stage core is solid, the second stage is liquid, and the third stage is cryogenic.
  • The indigenous cryogenic engine is CE-7.5, using liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
  • GSLV-D5 successfully used an indigenous cryogenic upper stage on 5 January 2014.
  • GSLV Mk II's published capability is about 2,250 kg to GTO.
  • GSLV-F16 launched NISAR into a Sun-synchronous polar orbit in July 2025.
  • Trap: GTO insertion, final satellite positioning and successful operation are separate milestones.

[ISRO, Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II, sections Vehicle Specifications, Technical Specification and About the Launch Vehicle, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, List of GSLV Launches, records through 30 October 2026, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, GSLV-F15/NVS-02 Mission, update dated 2 February 2025; ISRO, NVS-02 Spacecraft: On-Orbit Observations and Apex Committee Recommendations, 25 February 2026; ISRO, GSLV-F16/NISAR Mission, mission description dated 21 July 2025; ISRO, GSLV-F18/NVS-03 Mission, 30 October 2026 launch result; ISRO, Orbit Manoeuvring of NVS-03 Spacecraft, 31 October 2026.]

title: GSLV Mk II: Cryogenic Technology and Geosynchronous Transfer Missions

body:
Meaning and purpose of LVM3

LVM3 is India's heavy-lift orbital launch vehicle. It was previously designated GSLV Mark III (GSLV Mk III). Both names refer to the same launch-vehicle family, although LVM3 is the name used for its recent missions.

LVM3 was developed to launch heavier satellites and spacecraft than those normally carried by GSLV Mk II. It has been used for large communication satellites, groups of commercial satellites and India's Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 lunar missions.

Its designation can create confusion. GSLV Mk II and LVM3 are not the same rocket. LVM3 was formerly called GSLV Mk III, but it has a different first-stage arrangement and a more powerful cryogenic upper stage.

The 3 propulsion stages of LVM3

Despite being a heavy-lift rocket, LVM3 has 3 propulsion stages.

  1. First propulsion stage: 2 S200 solid strap-on boosters. These large solid motors provide the major thrust required during liftoff and early ascent.
  2. Second propulsion stage: L110 liquid core. This central liquid-propellant stage uses 2 Vikas engines to continue the ascent.
  3. Third propulsion stage: C25 cryogenic upper stage. This stage uses the indigenous CE-20 cryogenic engine and burns liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen to provide the final acceleration needed for orbital insertion.

The 2 S200 boosters together form the first propulsion stage in the standard description. They are not counted as 2 separate sequential stages. Thus, LVM3 is a 3-stage vehicle, not a 4-stage vehicle.

How LVM3 differs from GSLV Mk II

Both vehicles use a cryogenic upper stage, but their configurations and payload classes are different. GSLV Mk II has a solid first-stage core assisted by 4 liquid strap-ons and uses a CE-7.5 cryogenic upper-stage engine. LVM3 begins its propulsion sequence with 2 large solid S200 boosters, ignites the L110 liquid stage while the boosters are still firing, and later uses the more powerful CE-20 cryogenic upper-stage engine.

ISRO's detailed LVM3 specifications give an indicative capacity of about 4,000 kg to GTO and 8,000 kg to a 600 km LEO. These are orbit-specific reference capacities rather than identical limits for every possible mission profile. Later mission-specific performance figures can differ.

Engine pairing: GSLV Mk II uses CE-7.5 in its cryogenic upper stage. LVM3 uses CE-20 in its C25 cryogenic upper stage. Both are indigenous Indian cryogenic propulsion systems.

Important developmental milestones

On 18 December 2014, the LVM3-X/CARE mission successfully tested important aspects of the new launch vehicle in a suborbital experimental flight. A suborbital flight does not establish a sustained Earth orbit.

The first orbital developmental flight, GSLV Mk III-D1/GSAT-19, took place on 5 June 2017. It successfully launched the GSAT-19 communication satellite into GTO and marked a major step in India's indigenous heavy-lift capability.

The distinction between the 2014 experimental flight and the 2017 first orbital developmental flight is important when interpreting statements about LVM3's beginning.

Major missions launched by LVM3

DateMissionMain significance
22 July 2019LVM3-M1 / Chandrayaan-2Launched India's second lunar exploration mission.
23 October 2022LVM3-M2 / OneWeb India-1Launched 36 commercial communication satellites.
26 March 2023LVM3-M3 / OneWeb India-2Launched another 36 OneWeb satellites.
14 July 2023LVM3-M4 / Chandrayaan-3Launched India's third lunar exploration mission.
2 November 2025LVM3-M5 / CMS-03Launched a communication satellite weighing about 4,400 kg into GTO.
24 December 2025LVM3-M6 / BlueBird Block-2Launched a large commercial communication satellite into LEO.

The 2 OneWeb launches carried 72 satellites in total, with 36 satellites on each mission. They demonstrate LVM3's use for commercial deployment of multiple satellites into LEO rather than only for geosynchronous communication satellites.

Chandrayaan-3 and orbital insertion

On 14 July 2023, LVM3-M4 launched Chandrayaan-3 and injected the spacecraft into its planned initial Earth orbit. The spacecraft subsequently carried out manoeuvres to travel towards the Moon. Thus, the launch vehicle's successful Earth-orbit insertion and the spacecraft's later lunar operations were separate phases of the mission.

Connection with Gaganyaan

Gaganyaan is India's human-spaceflight programme. A human-rated LVM3 configuration has been developed for its planned crewed orbital missions. Human-rating involves meeting additional safety and reliability requirements associated with carrying people.

The existence of the human-rated configuration does not make every ordinary LVM3 satellite launch a human-spaceflight mission. In objective questions, the correct association is Gaganyaan with the human-rated LVM3 family.

Prelims focus

  • LVM3 is the current name of the launch-vehicle family earlier called GSLV Mk III.
  • It has 3 stages: S200 solid boosters, L110 liquid core and C25 cryogenic upper stage.
  • Its cryogenic upper-stage engine is CE-20, not CE-7.5.
  • Indicative payload capacity is about 4,000 kg to GTO and 8,000 kg to a 600 km LEO.
  • The first suborbital experimental flight was in 2014; the first orbital developmental flight was in 2017.
  • Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 were launched by LVM3.
  • Trap: LVM3's 2 solid boosters form its first propulsion stage; they do not make it a 4-stage vehicle.

[ISRO, LVM3 (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mk III), sections About the Launch Vehicle, Vehicle Specifications and Technical Specification, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, GSLV MkIII-D1/GSAT-19 Mission, mission details for 5 June 2017; ISRO, Launch Missions, records for LVM3 missions during 2019–2025, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, LVM3-M5/CMS-03 Mission, 2 November 2025 result; ISRO, LVM3-M6/BlueBird Block-2 Mission, December 2025 result.]

body:
Why does India need a small launch vehicle?

SSLV stands for Small Satellite Launch Vehicle. It was developed by ISRO to provide a dedicated launch option for relatively small spacecraft, including mini, micro and nanosatellites.

Small satellites are used for Earth observation, scientific measurements, technology demonstrations, educational projects and communication experiments. Some can travel as secondary payloads aboard larger rockets. However, a shared launch must accommodate the larger mission's schedule and orbital requirements.

A dedicated small launch vehicle can provide greater flexibility for customers whose satellite does not require the capacity of a larger rocket. SSLV was designed with features such as relatively low launch cost, reduced turnaround time, simplified launch preparations and the feasibility of launch-on-demand services. Launch-on-demand describes a design and service objective; it does not mean that a spacecraft can be launched instantaneously without preparation.

SSLV's propulsion configuration

SSLV has 3 solid-propellant stages followed by a small liquid-propulsion module for final velocity adjustment.

  1. SS1: The first solid stage provides thrust during liftoff and early ascent.
  2. SS2: The second solid stage continues acceleration after separation of the first stage.
  3. SS3: The third solid stage provides further acceleration towards the required orbital conditions.
  4. Velocity Trimming Module (VTM): A liquid-propulsion terminal module makes small adjustments to the spacecraft's velocity to improve the accuracy of orbital insertion.

ISRO describes SSLV as a 3-stage launch vehicle with a liquid-based terminal module. The VTM should therefore be identified separately rather than casually calling SSLV a conventional 4-stage rocket. SSLV does not use a cryogenic upper stage.

Payload class and orbital capability

SSLV's published design capability is approximately 500 kg to a 500 km planar low Earth orbit. It can also accommodate combinations of smaller satellites, subject to mission-specific mass and orbital requirements.

The 500 kg figure is associated with the specified 500 km orbital reference case. It should not be interpreted as a guaranteed capacity to every orbit, especially not to GTO.

SSLV is approximately 34 m tall with a liftoff mass of about 120 tonnes. These values help distinguish it from the much larger LVM3 and reinforce its intended small-satellite role.

The 3 developmental flights

DateMissionOutcome
7 August 2022SSLV-D1 / EOS-02First developmental flight; the satellites were not placed into their intended orbit.
10 February 2023SSLV-D2 / EOS-07Successful orbital insertion of EOS-07, Janus-1 and AzaadiSAT-2.
16 August 2024SSLV-D3 / EOS-08Successful third developmental flight; completed the SSLV Development Project.

Why SSLV-D2 was important

SSLV-D2 successfully placed 3 satellites into an approximately 450 km circular orbit with an inclination of about 37 degrees. The payloads were EOS-07, Janus-1 and AzaadiSAT-2.

AzaadiSAT-2 was a student-associated satellite project involving scientific payload contributions from girl students in India. Its presence on SSLV-D2 illustrates the usefulness of a small-satellite launcher for educational and technology-demonstration payloads.

The orbital inclination is also instructive: a 37-degree inclination is not a polar orbit. Thus, the fact that SSLV can launch small Earth-observation spacecraft does not mean every SSLV mission must use a polar or Sun-synchronous orbit.

Development status at the content cutoff

ISRO announced that the successful SSLV-D3 flight on 16 August 2024 completed the SSLV Development Project and enabled the transition towards operational missions involving Indian industry and NewSpace India Limited (NSIL).

At the 4 November 2026 content cutoff, ISRO's published SSLV launch list contained the 3 developmental flights D1, D2 and D3. Completion of the development project should not be confused with a claim that a later commercial orbital mission had already been flown.

Prelims focus

  • SSLV stands for Small Satellite Launch Vehicle.
  • It has 3 solid propulsion stages: SS1, SS2 and SS3.
  • A liquid-based Velocity Trimming Module provides final velocity corrections.
  • Its published reference capability is about 500 kg to a 500 km planar LEO.
  • SSLV-D1 in 2022 was unsuccessful; SSLV-D2 in 2023 was successful.
  • SSLV-D3 successfully launched EOS-08 on 16 August 2024 and completed the development project.
  • Trap: SSLV's liquid terminal module is not a cryogenic stage, and a 500 km orbit is not necessarily a polar orbit.

[ISRO, Small Satellite Launch Vehicle, sections Vehicle Configuration, Payload Capability and Technical Specification, accessed 4 November 2026; ISRO, SSLV-D1/EOS-02 Mission, flight outcome and mission description, 2022; ISRO, Successful Flight of Small Satellite Launch Vehicle, 10 February 2023; ISRO, SSLV-D3/EOS-08 Mission, 16 August 2024 result; ISRO, List of SSLV Launches, accessed 4 November 2026.]
